# The flow file

A flow is a YAML (or the same object as JSON) document, version 1: what the editor downloads and uploads, what the server keeps as a draft and what an agent reads and writes through the MCP.

## Shape

```yaml
version: 1 (the file format)
name: 'the flow name (the flow row keeps its own name: this one is informative)'
nodes:
    - id: unique in the flow; the Start is `start` and the End is `end` by convention
      type: a component type, or `start` / `end`
      label: 'optional: its name on the canvas and in the run record (default: the component name)'
      position: '{x, y} on the canvas (required; ~300 px apart left to right reads well)'
      config: the component's settings (see each component)
      outputKey: 'optional: the DATA key where it writes its result, for a component with a defaultOutputKey'
      override: 'optional, true: what it produces replaces DATA (only components with usesOverride)'
      disabled: 'optional, true: envelopes pass through it untouched'
      pinned: 'optional: {port: [DATA, ...]} replayed by test runs instead of running it'
      notes: 'optional: free text for people'
      loop: 'optional: the id of the Loop whose loop region holds this node directly (never on the Start or the End)'
      size: "a Loop's, {width, height}: where its Loop end card is on the canvas, as an offset from the Loop card's position"
edges:
    - source: node id
      sourcePort: out-N or error
      target: node id
      targetPort: in-N
groups:
    - id: string
      title: string
      color: string
      position: '{x, y}'
      size: '{width, height}'
```

## Ports

Inputs are in-0, in-1... and outputs out-0, out-1... in the order the component lists them. The error port is `error`, there only while the component's onError is divert. The Start has only out-0 and the End only in-0. A Loop has in-0 and out-0 (one edge each) facing outside, and two inner ports used from inside its loop region: `iteration-start` (a source, where each iteration starts) and `iteration-end` (a target, where the paths of an iteration finish), several edges each.

## The Start

Where every flow begins (not deletable, only an output). Its config holds whether the flow accepts an input (a webhook body, a calling flow's envelope, a test run's input), the input a test run uses by default, its type (a project script's type, `path#Name`) and the flow's parameters ($PARAMETERS). Without an input it yields one empty envelope; an input object is one envelope, a list one per item.

| Key                     | Label                | Kind        | Required | Default  | Notes                                                    |
| ----------------------- | -------------------- | ----------- | -------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `acceptsInput`          | Accepts input        | boolean     |          |          |                                                          |
| `inputType`             | Input type           | script-type |          |          | only when acceptsInput is `true`                         |
| `testInput`             | Default input (JSON) | code        |          |          | json; only when acceptsInput is `true`; e.g. `{"id": 1}` |
| `parameters`            | Parameters           | list        |          |          |                                                          |
| `parameters[].name`     | Name                 | text        | yes      |          | e.g. `since`                                             |
| `parameters[].type`     | Type                 | select      |          | `"text"` | one of `text`, `number`, `boolean`                       |
| `parameters[].default`  | Default              | text        |          |          |                                                          |
| `parameters[].required` | Required             | boolean     |          |          |                                                          |

## The End

Where every chain ends (only an input, several edges allowed). What reaches it is the flow's result: a calling Flow Invoker (wait) gets these envelopes.

## On error

Settings every component has, besides its own.

| Key       | Label    | Kind   | Required | Default   | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------- | -------- | ------ | -------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `onError` | On error | select |          | `"throw"` | What an envelope that fails in the component does: throw stops the run; continue goes on as it came in; divert goes out through the error port (`error`), with DATA.errors.; one of `throw`, `continue`, `divert` |

## Connections

A component that talks to a database or an API picks a connection profile of the workspace by its id in config.connection (list_connections gives them), or leaves it '' and fills the profile's fields in its own config (password-like fields always name a secret of the workspace). Any of them may set config.connection = '$dynamic' and name the profile in config.connectionName: a text, or an expression on $PARAMETERS, $VARIABLES and $SECRETS only (never the envelope: $DATA or its keys), evaluated once, so the component uses one connection for the whole run (e.g. "'Orders_' + $PARAMETERS.env"). To use another connection per item, a Flow Invoker calls a flow with the name as a parameter.

## Calling by expression

A Flow Invoker's flowId (or a Script Invoker's function) set to '$dynamic' takes the flow (function) from an expression on each envelope (flowPath / functionPath).

## Expressions

JavaScript expressions evaluated on each envelope (no statements, no `return`). Keep each one short: a value, a condition, a small formula. Logic with helpers, several statements or validation (an IIFE such as `(() => { ... })()`) reads better in a TypeScript component, which can import project scripts, or a Script Invoker; validate_flow warns about it (a suggestion, not an error).

- $<key>: a top-level key of the envelope DATA ($price, $customer.name, $items[0])
- $DATA: the whole DATA object
- $PARAMETERS.<name>: the Start parameters of the run
- $VARIABLES.<name>: the workspace's variables
- $SECRETS.<name> / $SECRETS['name']: the workspace's secret values (masked in the logs)
- $FLOW_CURRENT_RUN: the run, the same in every envelope: {id, mode, workspace, project, flow, startedAt, parentId?}
- $_loopIndex: in a Loop's loop region and its stop condition, the number of the iteration, 0 in the first; in nested Loops, that of the Loop whose region holds the component directly

### $FLOW_CURRENT_RUN

- `id`: the run's id (a flow a Flow Invoker calls runs as a run of its own, with its own id)
- `mode`: `validation` in a test run (the editor's Run, test_run: nothing is written outside), `execution` in a run for real (Run for real, a schedule, a webhook)
- `workspace`: the workspace's name
- `project`: the project's name
- `flow`: the flow's name, not its id (e.g. for a log or an error message: `$FLOW_CURRENT_RUN.flow`)
- `startedAt`: when the run started, ISO 8601 in UTC (e.g. 2026-11-09T00:45:54.260Z)
- `parentId`: only in a flow called by a Flow Invoker: the id of the run that called it

A setting of kind `value` is {value, expression}: expression false = the text as it is; true = an expression. In a list item marked `spread`, value and expression are the item's own keys ({name, value, expression}).

Output keys and field names: letters, digits and _, not starting with a digit, and not FLOW_CURRENT_RUN, PARAMETERS, SECRETS, VARIABLES, DATA.

## Rules

What `validate_flow` (and every run) checks:

- The file has version 1, a name, and nodes each with an id (unique), a type and a position.
- Exactly one Start and one End.
- Every edge connects two nodes of the flow, on ports their components have with their config (an edge on a port that is gone is an error).
- Every port takes several edges (an output copies each envelope to all of them; an input joins them in arrival order), except the Lookup: one edge on each of its inputs.
- The same two ports are not connected twice, and the Start never goes straight to the End.
- Edges out of the error port (`error`) only from a component whose onError is divert.
- No cycles: the flow is a directed acyclic graph (a Loop's iteration-start → … → iteration-end is a path inside its region, not a cycle).
- A loop region is closed: an edge joins two nodes with the same `loop` (a Loop's inner ports count as inside its region, its in-0 and out-0 as outside). The Start and End have no `loop`; a Continue with, a Next and a Break always have one; a `loop` names a Loop of the flow. Loops nest (a Loop with a `loop` is inside another), but never inside themselves, directly or through others.
- Every component type exists; each enabled component passes its own checks (required settings, names, SQL read only, and so on).
- Expressions compile (syntax only; unknown $variables are not an error, a key may come from upstream).
- Output keys and field names are valid names (letters, digits, _; not a reserved name).
- A Flow Invoker calls a flow of the same project; scripts are the project's. Connection profiles and secrets are the workspace's: one it does not have yet (by id, or a dynamic connection name known before the run) is a warning, not an issue: the draft is saved, and the run fails at that component until a person creates it.
- The Start's parameters have unique valid names and defaults of their type; its default input is valid JSON.
- Pinned outputs take at most 2 MB in all.

## Patterns

Ways to combine the components for common needs. Read them before designing a flow that does one of these.

### Do something once, after everything before it finished, knowing how it ended (a barrier)

A step must happen once and only after all the envelopes of a process were handled: advance a checkpoint, release a lock, report a failure, log a total. Also when nothing may come out of that process (an empty source).

- Use a Wait. Its `hold` input takes the envelope that goes on afterwards (e.g. the one that took the lock, with its ids); its `watch` input takes what comes out of the process: its output AND its error port (onError `divert`), both edges into `watch`.
- When `watch` ends (every component before it finished with every envelope) the held envelope goes on once with `$wait` = {status, envelopes, errors, firstError, last}: status `success` (envelopes arrived, no errors), `failure` (an envelope came from an error port) or `empty` (nothing arrived). It always answers, even when the process produced nothing.
- After it, a Router on `$wait.status`: success → advance the checkpoint; empty → release only (or advance, when an empty window is complete for you); failure → release, then a component that throws `$wait.firstError.message` so the run ends as failed.
- Without a status, a Limit with mode `bottom` (Last) and count 1 is the simplest barrier: it lets the last envelope through when its input ends, and nothing when no envelope arrives. With a Limit, keep onError `throw` on the components before it: an envelope that failed with `continue` or `divert` does not stop the run, so the barrier would still open.

### Incremental load with a checkpoint (watermark)

Each run reads only what changed since the last run that finished, from a source with a change date or an increasing key.

- Keep the checkpoint in a control table (one row per source: name, checkpoint). The run reads it first (a SQL Server or Redshift query) and computes the window end (`to`, e.g. now) once; the window is checkpoint → to. When the process calls another flow per source, pass the window as parameters.
- Read the window (a Pipeline or query with checkpoint < date <= to), process and write.
- Then a Wait (the barrier pattern): `hold` = the envelope with the source and the window, `watch` = the output and the error port of the processing. On success, a SQL Server Update of the control row: set checkpoint = `to`, Match on the source name, Expected values checkpoint = the old one (compare-and-set) and If no row matches = Error, so a concurrent run that moved it first is an error, not a silent overwrite.
- An empty window is safe either way: keeping the checkpoint, the next run reads from the same point up to its own `to`, covering it again. A failed run does not move it: the next run reads that window again, so the writes must be idempotent (an upsert or an update by key, not a plain insert).
- A Flow Invoker that waits passes on the envelopes that reach the End of the called flow as they arrive, and none when nothing reaches it: it is not a "finished" signal by itself. Its output and its error port into the `watch` of a Wait are: the Wait answers when the call finished, with how.

### One run at a time (a lock)

Two runs must not process the same source at once (a schedule that overlaps a slow run).

- A lock row in the control table (name, lockedBy, lockedUntil). At the start, read it; when it is free (lockedBy null) or expired (lockedUntil in the past), take it with a SQL Server Update: set lockedBy = the run, lockedUntil = now + a timeout, Expected values = the lockedBy and lockedUntil just read (compare-and-set) and If no row matches = Error. Two runs that read the same free lock: only one Update matches.
- At the end, after a Wait (the barrier pattern), release it whatever the status: set lockedBy and lockedUntil to null, Expected values lockedBy = the run.
- A run that is cancelled or whose worker stops does not release it: the expiry (lockedUntil) frees it for the next run. Choose a timeout longer than the slowest run.

## Example

```yaml
version: 1
name: Active customers to the CRM
nodes:
    - id: start
      type: start
      position: { x: 0, y: 0 }
      config:
          parameters:
              - { name: since, type: text, default: '2026-01-01' }
    - id: read
      type: sqlserver
      label: Read customers
      position: { x: 300, y: 0 }
      config:
          connection: <connection profile id>
          sql: |
              SELECT id, name, email FROM Customer WHERE updatedAt > @since
          parameters:
              - { name: since, value: $PARAMETERS.since, expression: true }
    - id: active
      type: filter
      position: { x: 600, y: 0 }
      config:
          condition: $email != null
    - id: send
      type: http-request
      position: { x: 900, y: 0 }
      config:
          connection: <connection profile id>
          method: POST
          url: { value: 'https://crm.example.com/contacts', expression: false }
          body: { value: '{name: $name, email: $email}', expression: true }
          onError: divert
    - id: failed
      type: log
      position: { x: 1200, y: 200 }
      config:
          level: warn
          message: '`could not send ${$id}: ${$errors[0].message}`'
    - id: end
      type: end
      position: { x: 1200, y: 0 }
      config: {}
edges:
    - { source: start, sourcePort: out-0, target: read, targetPort: in-0 }
    - { source: read, sourcePort: out-0, target: active, targetPort: in-0 }
    - { source: active, sourcePort: out-0, target: send, targetPort: in-0 }
    - { source: send, sourcePort: out-0, target: end, targetPort: in-0 }
    - { source: send, sourcePort: error, target: failed, targetPort: in-0 }
    - { source: failed, sourcePort: out-0, target: end, targetPort: in-0 }
```

## In a git repository

A workspace mirrored to git is a folder of its own on the environment's branch, in a public format (version 1) that the app, a person or another tool can write. The name of a project, folder, flow, connection or script is its path; its identity (`id`) is in its file, so a rename or a move is a move of the file. Every name is a valid file name everywhere (no `\ / : * ? " < > |`, no name Windows reserves, at most 64 characters, unique among its siblings whatever the case) and a path in the repository has at most 150 characters, so a clone on Windows works.

```text
.gitattributes                         # * text=auto eol=lf, written on the first export
<workspace>/
  workspace.yaml                       # format: 1
  connections/<connection name>.yaml   # id, type
  projects/<project name>/
    project.yaml                       # id, description, icon, color
    flows/<folder>/<flow name>.flow.yaml
    scripts/<script path>.ts
```

An empty folder of flows or of scripts keeps a `.gitkeep`. A file anywhere else is not part of the format.

### workspace.yaml

`format: 1`, the version of the format. A change to the format gets a new number.

### A connection

`connections/<connection name>.yaml` declares a connection: its `id` and its `type` only. Its configuration and credentials stay on each server, so no secret reaches git; a connection that arrives on a server from git is not configured there until someone configures it. Secrets and variables are not in the repository: a flow names them only.

```yaml
id: 0b6f3c1e-2a7d-4f0e-9c4b-5d8e1a2f3b4c
type: sqlserver
```

### project.yaml

The project's `id`, and its `description`, `icon` and `color`, each optional.

### A flow

`flows/<folder>/<flow name>.flow.yaml` is the flow file described above, with three differences: it has the flow's `id` (required); it has no `name`, which is the file name without `.flow.yaml`; it has no `pinned` outputs, which are test data and stay on the server. It may say `deployed: false` when the flow is not deployed; absent means `true`. A flow names the connections and the flows it calls by id, and scripts by path.

The server writes a flow once it has been deployed: the deployed version, or, after an undeploy, the version deployed last with `deployed: false`. A draft never reaches the repository, and an archived flow, folder or project leaves it.

### A script

`scripts/<script path>.ts`: the project's script, as it is. A script is identified by its path.

### The stable order

Every file the app writes is in one canonical order: a flow's nodes by id, its edges by source, target and then ports, its groups by id, and every key of a node's `config` from a to z (at every depth; lists keep their order). So writing a file the app read gives no diff, and two branches that each add a node rarely conflict. The app reads any order and any YAML formatting (flow style, quotes, CRLF line endings).

Comments are not part of the format: the app drops them when it writes a file. What a comment would say goes in a node's `notes`.

### Versions

A deploy makes a new version only when what the engine runs changed. A version's content hash leaves out `deployed`, the name, the canvas (positions, groups, notes), the pinned outputs, the order of nodes, edges and keys, and line endings (LF or CRLF): changing only `deployed` makes no new version.

### Validation of a tree

The app checks a whole workspace tree before applying it (`validateWorkspaceTree` in the core). An error refuses the tree whole, with the reasons listed: a file that is not valid YAML or does not match its schema (an unknown key included); an `id` missing or in two files of a kind; a `workspace.yaml` or a `project.yaml` missing; an edge to a node that does not exist; a call to a flow that is not in the workspace or to a script that is not in the project; a connection a flow uses and the workspace does not declare; a name breaking the rule above or a path too long; two names that differ only in case or Unicode normalization. A warning does not: a declared connection not configured on this server; a secret or variable a flow reads with no value on this server; a comment in a flow file; a repository without `.gitattributes`; a file that is not part of the format (it is left out).

### JSON Schemas

A JSON Schema for each file, for an editor to check the files as they are written:

| Schema                                                     | Files                        | For        |
| ---------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | ---------- |
| [`flow.schema.json`](schemas/flow.schema.json)             | `**/*.flow.yaml`             | flow       |
| [`project.schema.json`](schemas/project.schema.json)       | `**/projects/*/project.yaml` | project    |
| [`connection.schema.json`](schemas/connection.schema.json) | `**/connections/*.yaml`      | connection |
| [`workspace.schema.json`](schemas/workspace.schema.json)   | `**/workspace.yaml`          | workspace  |

In VS Code, with the YAML extension, in the settings:

```json
{
    "yaml.schemas": {
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flowtinus-hub/flowtinus/main/docs/schemas/flow.schema.json": ["**/*.flow.yaml"],
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flowtinus-hub/flowtinus/main/docs/schemas/project.schema.json": ["**/projects/*/project.yaml"],
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flowtinus-hub/flowtinus/main/docs/schemas/connection.schema.json": ["**/connections/*.yaml"],
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flowtinus-hub/flowtinus/main/docs/schemas/workspace.schema.json": ["**/workspace.yaml"]
    }
}
```
